questions.prompt: What happens first, right when a pathogen crosses into the body?
options: Memory cells immediately destroy it
Sensor cells in the tissue notice it doesn't belong and send out an alarm signal
Antibodies are already waiting to attack it
The body raises its temperature before anything else happens
questions.explanation: The immune response always starts with detection: sensor cells in the tissue recognize the pathogen's antigen markers as foreign and release chemical alarm signals, which is what calls white blood cells into action next.
questions.misconception: Students often assume the strongest tools (antibodies, memory cells) are ready from the very start, but those take stages to build — detection has to happen first.

questions.prompt: What do white blood cells do in the immune response?
options: They only carry oxygen around the body
They detect and fight pathogens, including engulfing invaders and helping coordinate the rest of the response
They are only active when you have a fever
They build new skin cells to close wounds
questions.explanation: White blood cells (leukocytes) are the immune system's active defenders — some, like macrophages, engulf pathogens directly, while others, like B cells and T cells, produce antibodies or kill infected cells.
questions.misconception: Students often mix up white blood cells with red blood cells; red blood cells carry oxygen, while white blood cells are dedicated to defense and don't carry oxygen at all.

questions.prompt: What is the job of an antibody?
options: It directly eats the entire pathogen whole
It binds tightly to a specific antigen on a pathogen, marking it for destruction
It turns into a new white blood cell
It lowers your body temperature to fight infection
questions.explanation: Antibodies are shaped to match one specific antigen, like a key fitting a lock. Once attached, they tag the pathogen so other immune cells can destroy it — they don't destroy it by themselves.
questions.misconception: Students often confuse antibodies with white blood cells themselves; antibodies are proteins made by plasma cells (a type of white blood cell), not cells that act on their own.

questions.prompt: Once a pathogen is tagged with antibodies, how does the body finish clearing it out?
options: The tag makes the pathogen dissolve on its own
Phagocyte cells recognize the antibody tags and break the pathogen apart
The pathogen turns into a memory cell
Antibodies alone break the pathogen apart without help from other cells
questions.explanation: Antibodies mark the pathogen but don't destroy it themselves — phagocyte cells recognize the antibody tags, engulf the marked pathogen, and break it apart, clearing the infection.
questions.misconception: A common assumption is that antibodies do the destroying by themselves; in reality, antibodies tag and phagocyte cells carry out the actual destruction.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't your body usually get chickenpox a second time after having it once?
options: The virus disappears from the planet after one infection
Skin becomes permanently thicker and blocks the virus
Memory cells from the first infection recognize the virus and respond much faster the second time
White blood cells run out of pathogens to fight so they multiply forever
questions.explanation: After an infection, the immune system keeps memory B cells and T cells that recognize that exact pathogen. If it returns, these memory cells trigger a faster, stronger response — often stopping the infection before symptoms appear.
questions.misconception: A common misconception is that the pathogen is gone from the world or that skin/organs physically change to block it — immunity is about the immune system's memory, not a physical barrier upgrade.

questions.prompt: Why do vaccines help prevent disease?
options: They physically block germs from entering the body like a shield
They kill all germs in the environment around you
They train the immune system to create memory cells for a pathogen without causing the full disease
They replace your white blood cells with stronger ones
questions.explanation: Vaccines expose the immune system to a harmless piece or weakened version of a pathogen's antigens. This triggers antibody production and memory cell formation, so the body is ready to respond quickly if it meets the real pathogen later.
questions.misconception: A frequent misunderstanding is that vaccines act as a physical barrier or that they contain the full, dangerous disease — most vaccines contain no live, dangerous pathogen at all, only enough of a signature to train memory cells.
